This very thing, however, seems probable to REISKE in his Conjecturis in Iobum et Proverbia Salomonis, Leipzig 1779, p. 162, who cannot persuade himself that רננים is a name of the ostrich. His words are: "But there is no great need for that name to be expressed. For it is the custom of the Arabs to discourse at length on some thing and yet not to name it. Asked why they do so, they answer, لعلم السمع بها [li-ʿilm al-samʿ bihā], because the hearer knows it, since the hearer, and hence also the reader, can very easily grasp from the character of the epithets, the predicates and the description, and from the whole thread of the discourse, what the subject is. [Cf. the same Reiske in the notes on Tarafa's Moallaka, p. 86.] Our Job himself used this figure above, ch. XXVI, 2-5, where he describes God without naming him. Compare XL, 10." So Reiske, with whom Doederlein in his Scholia ad Libros Poeticos V. T. on the passage, and Dathe agree; they translate these words thus: There is one that exults with whirring wings, etc. Whether this is to be preferred to the interpretation that Bochart will give presently, let each judge for himself. I pass over the bold conjectures of Reiske and Michaelis, by which they needlessly disturb the received text. Whoever wishes to know them should consult the authors themselves.

The asseverative sense of the particle אם, which is perhaps the primary one, seems rather to be derived from the meaning to tend, to aim at, to have a purpose, which is found in the Arabic verb أَمَّ [amma], which ALB. SCHULTENS compared on Iob. XLII, 8, p. 1214. Cf. STORR, Observatt. ad Analog. et Synt. Hebr. p. 348, note *).

I refrain from reviewing the opinions, or rather the guesses, of others in interpreting this verse, since this has already been done sufficiently by SCHULTENS in his Commentary on the passage, p. 1118 ff. The vain conjectures of Schmidt and Cocceius have also been refuted by TYMPIUS in his Annotationibus et Vindiciis on Noldii Concordantt. Particularr. p. 903 b, note 1460.
